stem.en: Malware is short for:

explanation.en: Malware is any software designed to damage, disrupt or gain unauthorised access to a computer system.

stem.en: Which malware is a standalone program that copies itself across a network without needing a host file?

explanation.en: A worm is self-replicating and self-contained; it spreads over networks on its own. A virus needs to attach itself to a host program or file.

stem.en: Ransomware:

options.en: Records every key the user presses
Blocks access to data, usually by encrypting it, and demands payment to restore it
Speeds up the computer by deleting temporary files

explanation.en: Ransomware locks or encrypts the victim’s data and demands a ransom. WannaCry (2017) is a well-known example.

stem.en: A program that looks like a useful game but secretly opens a back door for an attacker is a:

explanation.en: Like the wooden horse of Troy, a Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software. Unlike viruses and worms it does not replicate itself.

solution.en: Like the wooden horse of Troy, a Trojan disguises itself as legitimate software.
Unlike viruses and worms it does not replicate itself.

stem.en: Which statement about a computer virus is correct?

options.en: It attaches itself to a host file and spreads when the infected file is run or shared
It spreads only through hardware faults
It never needs a host program

explanation.en: A virus is a piece of code that inserts itself into other programs or files; it becomes active when the host is executed.

stem.en: Software that secretly records a user’s activity and sends the information to someone else is called:

explanation.en: Spyware collects information (browsing habits, passwords, card numbers) without the user’s knowledge and sends it to a remote party.

stem.en: A keylogger:

options.en: Locks the keyboard until a ransom is paid
Records the keys pressed on the keyboard, capturing passwords and messages

explanation.en: Keyloggers (software or hardware) record keystrokes. Using an on-screen (virtual) keyboard for passwords helps defeat software keyloggers.

stem.en: Malware that bombards the user with unwanted pop-up advertisements is:

explanation.en: Adware displays unwanted ads; it may also track the user to choose the ads.

stem.en: Which of these is NOT a common way in which malware spreads?

options.en: Typing a document in a word processor that came pre-installed
Opening an attachment in a spam email
Plugging in an infected pen drive
Downloading pirated software from the internet

explanation.en: Malware spreads through downloads, spam email attachments, removable storage and network propagation. Ordinary use of genuine software is not a route.

solution.en: Malware spreads through downloads, spam email attachments, removable storage and network propagation.
Ordinary use of genuine software is not a route.

stem.en: Typing a password with an on-screen (virtual) keyboard mainly protects against:

explanation.en: A software keylogger records physical keystrokes; clicking keys on an on-screen keyboard avoids them.

stem.en: Signature-based detection in an antivirus works by:

options.en: Comparing files with a database of known malware patterns (virus definitions)

explanation.en: A signature is a unique pattern of a known malware. The antivirus compares files with its signature database, which must be kept updated.

stem.en: Unwanted bulk messages, usually email, sent to many people are called:

explanation.en: Spam is unsolicited bulk messaging, often advertising and sometimes carrying malware or phishing links.

stem.en: Running a suspicious program in an isolated virtual environment to watch its behaviour is called:

explanation.en: A sandbox lets the antivirus observe what a program does without letting it harm the real system.

stem.en: Why must the virus definitions of an antivirus be updated regularly?

options.en: Old definitions slow down the internet
Definitions expire by law every month
New malware appears every day, and signature-based detection only recognises malware already in its database

explanation.en: Signature-based detection cannot catch malware it has no signature for, so the database must keep up with new threats.

solution.en: Signature-based detection cannot catch malware it has no signature for, so the database must keep up with new threats.

stem.en: Heuristic detection in an antivirus:

options.en: Works only after the computer is infected for a week
Flags programs whose code or behaviour looks like malware, even without a known signature
Is another name for a firewall

explanation.en: Heuristics look for suspicious features or behaviour, so they can catch new variants of malware.

stem.en: The main difference between HTTP and HTTPS is that HTTPS:

options.en: Is faster because it sends no headers
Encrypts the data exchanged between the browser and the server

explanation.en: HTTPS is HTTP over SSL/TLS: data is encrypted in transit, so an eavesdropper sees only scrambled data. A padlock icon shows an HTTPS connection.

stem.en: A firewall:

options.en: Monitors incoming and outgoing network traffic and allows or blocks it according to security rules

explanation.en: A firewall is a network security system (hardware or software) that filters traffic using predefined rules.

stem.en: Cookies are:

options.en: Small text files that a website stores in the browser to remember information about the user

explanation.en: Cookies remember logins, preferences and cart items. Third-party cookies can be used to track users across websites.

stem.en: Why should you not enter your card details on a site whose address starts with http:// (no padlock)?

options.en: The browser will delete the card
The data travels as plain text and can be read by anyone who intercepts it

explanation.en: Without encryption, the details can be captured on the way. Sensitive data should be sent only over HTTPS.

stem.en: An ethical (white-hat) hacker:

options.en: Breaks into systems for personal gain
Finds security weaknesses with permission so that they can be fixed

explanation.en: Ethical hackers test systems with the owner’s consent. Black-hat hackers (crackers) break in illegally for gain or damage.

stem.en: A Denial of Service (DoS) attack:

options.en: Floods a server or network with requests so that legitimate users cannot use it

explanation.en: DoS exhausts resources (bandwidth, memory, processing) so that the service is denied to genuine users.

stem.en: In a DDoS attack, the flood of traffic comes from:

options.en: Many compromised computers (a botnet of zombies) at the same time

explanation.en: Distributed DoS uses many infected machines controlled by the attacker, which makes it much harder to block.

stem.en: Unauthorised real-time interception of a private communication, such as a phone call or video conference, is called:

explanation.en: Eavesdropping is listening in on a private conversation as it happens. Snooping is the secret capture and analysis of network traffic, which may be examined later.

solution.en: Eavesdropping is listening in on a private conversation as it happens.
Snooping is the secret capture and analysis of network traffic, which may be examined later.

stem.en: A cracker is best described as:

options.en: A person who breaks into computer systems illegally, with malicious intent

explanation.en: Crackers are black-hat hackers: they gain unauthorised access to steal, damage or demand money.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): A worm can spread through a network even if no user opens an infected file.
Reason (R): A worm is a standalone program that replicates itself without needing a host program.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: Because a worm is self-contained and self-replicating, it does not wait for a user to run a host file: R explains A.

stem.en:
Assertion (A): A website that uses HTTPS is protected against every kind of malware.
Reason (R): HTTPS encrypts the data travelling between the browser and the web server.

options.en: Both A and R are true, and R is the correct explanation of A.
Both A and R are true, but R is not the correct explanation of A.
A is true, but R is false.
A is false, but R is true.

explanation.en: HTTPS only encrypts data in transit; a site using HTTPS can still host malware. So A is false and R is true.

stem.en: Which type of malware has attacked the café?

explanation.en: Files locked (encrypted) and a payment demanded to unlock them is the signature of ransomware.

passage.en: Raghav runs a small cyber café in Mysuru with ten computers. One morning all files on the shared drive are renamed with a strange extension, and a note demands ₹50,000 in cryptocurrency to unlock them. He finds that an employee had opened an email attachment called "Invoice.pdf.exe" the previous evening. The café’s antivirus had not been updated for six months, and there was no backup.

stem.en: Which step would best have protected the café against losing its data?

options.en: Keeping an updated antivirus and regular offline backups, and not opening unknown attachments
Turning off the monitors at night

explanation.en: Updated antivirus and caution with attachments prevent infection, and offline backups let data be restored without paying.

stem.en:
Match the malware with its behaviour:
(i) Virus  (ii) Worm  (iii) Trojan  (iv) Ransomware
(a) disguises itself as useful software  (b) encrypts data and demands money  (c) attaches to a host file  (d) self-replicates over a network

explanation.en: Virus → attaches to a host; worm → self-replicates over networks; Trojan → disguised as useful software; ransomware → encrypts and demands ransom.

solution.en: Virus → attaches to a host; worm → self-replicates over networks; Trojan → disguised as useful software; ransomware → encrypts and demands ransom.

stem.en:
Which of the following statements are true?
A. A firewall can be hardware or software.
B. HTTPS encrypts data between browser and server.
C. Cookies are executable programs that spread like viruses.
D. Third-party cookies can be used to track users across websites.

explanation.en: C is false: cookies are small text files, not executable programs. A, B and D are true.

stem.en: A password uses only the 26 lowercase letters and has 6 characters. An attacker can try 10⁶ passwords per second. In the worst case, a brute-force attack takes about:

explanation.en: 26⁶ = 308,915,776 passwords ÷ 10⁶ per second ≈ 309 seconds ≈ 5.1 minutes. Short, simple passwords are weak.
